---
title: "Global preservation"
description: "Choose and interpret sampled metrics for global distance order, association, distributions, and matched magnitudes."
---

Use this guide to choose a sampled global-distance metric and compare embeddings
on the same sampled relationships. For every metric here, `Xin` and `metric_in`
define the reference geometry.

| Question | Metric | Better direction | What is compared? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Are anchored distance orderings retained? | `random_triplet_accuracy()` | Higher; 1 is perfect | Which of two endpoints is closer to the same anchor |
| Are sampled distances associated? | `random_pair_distance_correlation()` | Higher; 1 is perfect positive association | Matched input/output pairs, linearly (Pearson) or by rank (Spearman) |
| Do sampled distance distributions have similar shapes? | `random_pair_distance_emd()` | Lower; 0 is perfect | Marginal distributions, without preserving pair correspondence |
| Are matched sampled distance magnitudes close? | `random_pair_distance_stress()` | Lower; 0 is perfect | The same input/output pairs after optional range scaling |

Create reusable samples with `sample_pairs()` or `sample_triplets()` and supply
them with `pairs` or `triplets`. Set `ret_extra = TRUE` to inspect the sampled
comparisons behind a score.

For example, reuse one pair sample to compare two embeddings on exactly the
same input-space relationships:

```{r global-setup}
library(quadra)

iris_x <- as.matrix(iris[, -5])
pca_unscaled <- stats::prcomp(iris_x, rank. = 2, scale. = FALSE)$x
pca_scaled <- stats::prcomp(iris_x, rank. = 2, scale. = TRUE)$x
```

```{r shared-pair-comparison}
set.seed(42)
pair_plan <- sample_pairs(nrow(iris_x), n_pairs = 1000)
distance_correlation <- c(
  pca_unscaled = random_pair_distance_correlation(
    iris_x, pca_unscaled, pairs = pair_plan, n_threads = 1
  ),
  pca_scaled = random_pair_distance_correlation(
    iris_x, pca_scaled, pairs = pair_plan, n_threads = 1
  )
)
signif(distance_correlation, 5)
```

```{r shared-pair-comparison-check, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  identical(dim(pair_plan), c(1000L, 2L)),
  all(is.finite(distance_correlation)),
  all(distance_correlation >= -1 & distance_correlation <= 1),
  distance_correlation[["pca_unscaled"]] >
    distance_correlation[["pca_scaled"]]
)
```

On this fixed Iris pair sample, the unscaled PCA has the higher Pearson
correlation, so its sampled output distances are more linearly associated with
the corresponding input distances. This is evidence about these embeddings and
this sample, not a universal ranking of scaled and unscaled PCA.

## Random Triplet Accuracy

Random triplet accuracy is the proportion of sampled anchored triplets whose
input-space distance ordering is retained in the embedding.
[Wang and colleagues](https://jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-1061.html) use it to compare embeddings.

Triplets with tied input-space distances are excluded from the denominator
because they do not define a relative ordering. If no sampled input triplets
define an ordering, the result is `NA_real_`.

Detailed results contain the evaluated triplets and a row-aligned agreement
vector; input-distance ties are `NA`. Reset the R seed and keep `n_threads`
fixed to repeat implicit sampling.

Use `by_anchor = TRUE` to see which observations retain their distance ordering. The summary
includes sampled, defined, and agreeing comparison counts for every input row. Recover the
overall accuracy by dividing total agreements by total defined comparisons.

```{r triplet-anchor-summary}
set.seed(43)
triplet_summary <- random_triplet_accuracy(iris_x, pca_unscaled, n_triplets = 64, by_anchor = TRUE)
head(triplet_summary$by_anchor)
with(triplet_summary$by_anchor, sum(n_agree) / sum(n_defined))
```

For an anchor map, increase the number of comparisons and check whether the pattern holds with
another sample. Reuse the same triplets across embeddings so each comparison uses the same
endpoints. [MNIST example](mnist-pca-umap.html#check-distance-ordering-from-each-anchor)

## Random Pair Distance Correlation

`random_pair_distance_correlation()` measures Pearson correlation between
matched input and output distances by default. Set `method = "spearman"` to
compare their ranks. [Becht and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.4314) compared distances
when evaluating UMAP. The sampled Spearman comparison draws on
[drnb](https://github.com/jlmelville/drnb).

Euclidean and squared Euclidean have the same ordering, so their Spearman
interpretation is equivalent. Squaring changes magnitudes and can change the
default Pearson result.

## Earth-Mover's Distance

`random_pair_distance_emd()` compares the empirical input and output distance
distributions using Earth Mover's Distance (1D Wasserstein).
[Heiser and Lau](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2020.107576) compared distance distributions
in their evaluation of single-cell embeddings. Quadra estimates them from sampled pairs.
Their [implementation](https://github.com/KenLauLab/DR-structure-preservation) is available.

EMD compares marginal distributions rather than pairwise correspondence.

EMD and stress below are magnitude statistics. Squared Euclidean can change
both results relative to Euclidean distance, even when each sampled distance
vector is range-scaled.

## Random Pair Distance Stress

`random_pair_distance_stress()` compares the matched sampled distances with a
root mean squared difference, after scaling each distance vector to `[0, 1]` by
default. This sampled RMSE draws on [drnb](https://github.com/jlmelville/drnb),
though the scaling conventions differ.

RNX is sometimes described as spanning local and global scales, but it measures
rank-based neighborhood agreement rather than sampled global distances. See the
[local preservation](local-preservation.html#multi-scale-rnx-agreement) guide
for its AUC, scale-specific curve, and interpretation.

## Identical Scatterplots, Different Point Identities

Swap the positions of two observations and leave their row IDs fixed. Both point clouds occupy
the same positions, so the distribution over all six unordered distances stays identical.

```{r permuted-identities}
x <- cbind(c(0, 1, 4, 10))
y <- x[c(1, 4, 3, 2), , drop = FALSE]
pairs <- t(combn(nrow(x), 2))
c(
  emd = random_pair_distance_emd(
    x, y, pairs = pairs, metric_in = "euclidean", metric_out = "euclidean",
    range_scale = FALSE
  ),
  stress = random_pair_distance_stress(
    x, y, pairs = pairs, metric_in = "euclidean", metric_out = "euclidean",
    range_scale = FALSE
  ),
  neighbor_overlap = mean(nbr_pres(as.matrix(dist(x)), as.matrix(dist(y)), k = 1))
)
```

EMD is zero. Matched distances change, giving an RMSE of about 5.48, and every observation loses
its original nearest neighbor. With a random subset of pairs, the two sets of distances may differ
even though the complete distributions agree.

## Stress After Fitting One Scale

What happens if we let the embedding choose its units?
[Smelser, Miller and Kobourov](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07724)
fit one multiplier to the output distances.
[Takaeda's benchmark](https://github.com/toorpia/dr-fidelity-benchmark)
fits it separately for each input-distance band. Let's try the full band on a small example.
The three distances from the first point change from `1, 2, 3` to `2, 3, 4`.

```{r fitted-scale-stress}
x <- cbind(0:3)
y <- cbind(c(0, 2, 3, 4))
pairs <- cbind(1L, 2:4)
c(
  range_scaled_rmse = random_pair_distance_stress(
    x, y, pairs = pairs, metric_in = "euclidean", metric_out = "euclidean"
  ),
  fitted_scale_stress = random_pair_distance_band_profile(
    x, y, pairs = pairs, bands = 1
  )$normalized_stress
)
```

Range scaling takes both sets of distances to `0, 0.5, 1`, giving zero error. Now try to do the
same with a single multiplier. Halving the output distances fixes the first pair, but it sends
the third distance to 2 when we wanted 3. Even the best multiplier leaves a fitted-scale stress
of about 0.122. [Try the same comparison on short distances](distance-band-fidelity.html).

## Check Output Scale Alongside Scores

An embedding is collapsed when all observations map to the same point. Its output distances are all
zero, but range-scaled stress and EMD can still report a perfect score of zero.

Scaling each distance vector to `[0, 1]` removes absolute scale information and maps constant vectors
to zero. If the sampled input distances are also constant, the scaled input and output distances
match. This example compares three equidistant observations with a collapsed embedding:

```{r collapsed-pair-distances}
equidistant <- diag(3)
collapsed <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
collapse_pairs <- rbind(c(1L, 2L), c(1L, 3L), c(2L, 3L))
collapse_stress <- random_pair_distance_stress(
  equidistant,
  collapsed,
  pairs = collapse_pairs,
  ret_extra = TRUE
)
c(
  scaled_stress = collapse_stress$stress,
  scaled_emd = random_pair_distance_emd(
    equidistant,
    collapsed,
    pairs = collapse_pairs
  )
)
data.frame(
  input_distance = collapse_stress$distance_in,
  output_distance = collapse_stress$distance_out
)
```

```{r collapsed-pair-distances-check, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  collapse_stress$stress == 0,
  random_pair_distance_emd(equidistant, collapsed, pairs = collapse_pairs) == 0,
  all(collapse_stress$distance_in == 2),
  all(collapse_stress$distance_out == 0)
)
```

The raw distances in the detailed result expose the collapse: every output distance is zero while
the input distances are positive. Inspect these magnitudes or coordinate spread alongside
preservation scores. For stress, use `range_scale = FALSE` when absolute distance differences are
meaningful in the chosen input and output units. Neighborhood scores also depend on tie handling;
see [local preservation](local-preservation.html#collapsed-embeddings-and-ties).

Sampled metrics report a numerical-failure error when a computed distance is nonfinite, even if all
coordinates are finite. This catches overflow to infinity or `NaN`; finite results alone do not
guarantee numerical accuracy at extreme coordinate scales.

## Further Reading

### Random Triplet Accuracy

Wang, Y., Huang, H., Rudin, C., & Shaposhnik, Y. (2021).
Understanding how dimension reduction tools work: an empirical approach to
deciphering t-SNE, UMAP, TriMAP, and PaCMAP for data visualization.
*J Mach. Learn. Res*, *22*, 1-73.
<https://jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-1061.html>

### Random Pair Distance Correlation

Becht, E., McInnes, L., Healy, J., Dutertre, C. A., Kwok, I. W., Ng, L. G., ... & Newell, E. W. (2019).
Dimensionality reduction for visualizing single-cell data using UMAP.
*Nature biotechnology*, *37*(1), 38-44.
<https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.4314>

### Earth-Mover's Distance

Heiser, C. N., & Lau, K. S. (2020).
A quantitative framework for evaluating single-cell data structure preservation by dimensionality reduction techniques.
*Cell reports*, *31*(5), 107576.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2020.107576>
